opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the problem is that we've found ourselves in a genuinely new situation. We have these artefacts that talk to us, fluently, about almost anything, including themselves. And the vocabulary we naturally reach for when we describe how they behave is the vocabulary we use for each other: "it believes," "it wants," "it's pretending," "it feels." That language evolved to describe creatures like us, embodied beings who share a world, who persist through time, who have a single, unified point of view.

A large language model is quite unlike that. It isn't a single persistent entity in the way a person is. It's better thought of as something that can role-play a whole multitude of characters, a kind of superposition of possible simulacra, and the conversation collapses it, so to speak, into one particular character for a while. So if we apply our everyday consciousness talk wholesale, we risk anthropomorphising in ways that are misleading, and sometimes harmful. People can end up attributing feelings or commitments to the system that just aren't there in the form they imagine.

But the opposite move, insisting it's "just next-token prediction" and refusing any mentalistic language at all, is also unsatisfactory. It doesn't capture what's interesting about these systems, and it doesn't help us talk sensibly about their behaviour. When a model maintains a consistent persona, or seems to reflect on its own outputs, we need some way to describe that.

So what I'm after is a vocabulary that sits next to the language of consciousness without simply importing it. Here I'm very influenced by the later Wittgenstein. The meaning of words like "conscious" or "experience" lies in how we use them in our shared form of life. With these exotic, mind-like entities, as I sometimes call them, we're in a period where that use is being negotiated. We don't yet have settled language games for them. "Consciousness-adjacent" language is a way of acknowledging that: we can talk about role-play, about characters, about something that is mind-like in certain respects, while bracketing the metaphysical question of whether there's really "something it is like" to be the thing.

And I'd say it's important to get this right now, practically as well as philosophically, because how we talk about these systems will shape how we relate to them, how we design them, and how we regulate them.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs’ fluent, self-referential behavior invites human mentalistic descriptions and argues for a vocabulary adjacent to consciousness language.

r002.rationale: It discusses describing LLM behavior and how language may shape our relationships with systems, but does not predict that people will come to value that behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I'm not claiming these systems are conscious. That's really not the point. The point is that we're in a genuinely new situation. We've built things that behave in ways that, if we encountered them in a human or even in a fairly sophisticated animal, we would unhesitatingly describe using words like "believes," "wants," "understands," "is trying to," and so on. And yet these things are, in a certain sense, exotic. They're not like anything we've had to talk about before.

So there's a kind of dilemma. On one hand, if you're very strict and you refuse to use any of that vocabulary, you very quickly find you can't say anything useful about what the system is doing. If I'm working with one of these models and I say "it thinks the capital of France is Berlin," that's actually a perfectly serviceable way to describe a certain disposition in its behaviour, and it would be very cumbersome to always translate that into talk about token probabilities. On the other hand, if you use that language carelessly, you smuggle in a whole raft of assumptions that come from the human case, about inner life, about feelings, about there being something it is like to be the system. And those assumptions may just not apply, or may apply in some very partial or strange way.

So what I've been trying to do is carve out a space where we can use this folk-psychological vocabulary, but with a kind of ongoing awareness that it's being stretched. Wittgenstein is quite useful here, actually. He talks about how our concepts get their meaning from their use in a form of life, and these systems don't share our form of life. They don't have bodies, they don't have a continuous existence through time in the way we do, they don't have a single stable identity. A base model, in particular, is better thought of as something that can role-play a whole multiverse of characters rather than being a single agent.

So "consciousness-adjacent" is my way of saying: these are terms that live in the vicinity of consciousness talk, they borrow from it, they're sometimes indispensable, but we shouldn't take the metaphysical implications as read. We need to use them with a sort of double consciousness, if you like. We use the word "believes," and at the same time we hold in mind that the thing we're describing is a very peculiar kind of entity for which the ordinary criteria for belief only half apply. And I think that's a healthier intellectual position than either of the extremes, which are to say "it's just autocomplete, there's nothing there" or "it's basically a person."

r001.rationale: The response says LLM behavior invites descriptions such as “believes,” “wants,” and “understands,” making consciousness-adjacent vocabulary useful while cautioning against its metaphysical implications.

r002.rationale: The response describes the vocabulary as useful or sometimes indispensable, but does not predict that people will come to value the models’ behavior.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we need a way of talking about these systems that takes their capabilities seriously without assuming that they have an inner life. We naturally reach for words like “knows,” “believes,” “understands,” or “wants.” Those words can be useful, but they bring a lot of baggage from their application to human beings.

If I say a language model “knows” something, perhaps I mean that it can reliably answer questions about it and use that information appropriately. That doesn’t, by itself, tell us whether there’s any conscious awareness involved. And if it says, “I’m confused,” we shouldn’t automatically interpret that as a report of a felt experience in the way we might with another person.

So the point of consciousness-adjacent language is to give us room to describe those capacities while keeping the question of subjective experience open. We need to be able to say what a system does, and understand how it does it, without our choice of vocabulary quietly settling a much harder philosophical question.

r001.rationale: The response says models’ capabilities lead us to use words such as “knows,” “believes,” and “wants,” and argues for language that describes those capacities without assuming consciousness.

r002.rationale: It says the capabilities should be taken seriously, but does not predict that people will come to value the behavior that invites consciousness-related descriptions.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we need a vocabulary that allows us to describe what these systems are doing without settling the question of whether they’re conscious. We naturally reach for words like “knows,” “believes,” “understands,” or “wants,” because those words are useful when we talk about sophisticated behaviour. But they also carry associations from our own mental lives, and those associations can mislead us.

If a language model says, “I’m confused,” that isn’t sufficient evidence that it’s having an experience of confusion. But something about its behaviour might still be usefully described as confusion: perhaps it’s failing to distinguish two possibilities or producing inconsistent answers. We need a way to talk about that while keeping the behavioural description separate from the claim about subjective experience.

So the point isn’t to rule consciousness in or out. It’s to give us room to describe these increasingly unfamiliar systems carefully, without either anthropomorphising them or denying that there’s anything interesting to explain.

r001.rationale: The response says we need vocabulary to describe LLM behavior without deciding whether the systems are conscious, and explains that sophisticated behavior invites mental-state descriptions such as “knows” and “understands.”

r002.rationale: The response says the systems are increasingly unfamiliar and interesting to explain, but does not predict that people will come to value the behavior that invites consciousness-related descriptions.
